title: Microsoft (MSFT.US) has released its next-generation AI image model, MAI Image 2.7, which ranks second only to models developed by OpenAI in terms of performance. - 富途牛牛
content: On Tuesday, Microsoft unveiled its latest AI image model, MAI Image 2.7, further strengthening its technological footprint in the generative AI space. Zhitong Finance APP learned that Microsoft (MSFT.US) unveiled its latest AI image model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, further strengthening its technological footprint in the generative AI space. According to third-party evaluation results, the model ranks second on the AI image model leaderboard, trailing only OpenAI's GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, and outperforming Google's (GOOGL.US, GOOG.US) related AI models as well as Microsoft's previous-generation MAI-Image-2.6. Microsoft stated that MAI Image 2.7 is now available on platforms such as Arena, Artificial Analysis, and MAI Playground, allowing users to experience the new model's features. According to Microsoft's official blog, MAI Image 2.7 outperformed its predecessor, MAI-Image-2.6, across all 10 application scenarios and 7 image-editing operations evaluated by Artificial Analysis. Specifically, the new model achieves industry-leading performance in areas such as image enhancement and restoration, inference-based image editing, scene and style adjustment, and text and symbol editing. Among these, scene and style editing is the area where MAI Image 2.7 excels most, with an Elo score that outpaces the second-ranked model in this category by 24 points, highlighting Microsoft's technological advances in complex image-editing tasks. It is worth noting that Microsoft has, for the first time, made available the image-editing features of MAI Image 2.7, while the text-to-image generation feature has not yet been officially launched. Microsoft stated that the relevant features will go live in the near future. As competition in generative AI technology continues to intensify, image generation and editing have become one of the key areas where tech giants are focusing their efforts. With the launch of its new-generation AI image model, Microsoft has demonstrated that it is steadily strengthening its capabilities in developing proprietary AI models and expanding the application scenarios of its AI technologies by enhancing image-editing performance. From a market performance perspective, as of press time, Microsoft's stock price rose slightly by 0.35%, trading at $534.44. Overall, MAI Image 2.7's performance in third-party evaluations reflects Microsoft's ongoing advancements in the field of AI image technology. With the upcoming release of text-to-image capabilities, the market will closely monitor the new model's real-world application performance and its potential to bolster Microsoft's competitiveness in the generative AI market. title: Alphabet & Microsoft Earnings Preview: AI Cloud Growth Takes Center Stage - TradingView
content: Magnificent Seven giants Alphabet GOOGL) and Microsoft MSFT) are set to report their quarterly results after market hours on Wednesday, October 28, putting two of the world's largest artificial intelligence and cloud computing companies in the spotlight. With AI spending reaching unprecedented levels, Wall Street will be watching whether accelerating cloud demand, new AI products, and enterprise adoption can justify their massive infrastructure investments. Alphabet's Q3 Expectations: Google Cloud, Gemini & AI Search The Zacks Consensus Estimate calls for Alphabet to post Q3 earnings of $2.94 per share, up more than 2% year over year, with revenue excluding traffic acquisition costs (ex-TAC) projected to jump nearly 28% to $111.8 billion. Investors will be particularly focused on Google Cloud, which posted exceptional 82% revenue growth in Q2, alongside the continued expansion of Google's Search advertising and YouTube businesses. Based on Zacks estimates, Google Cloud revenue is projected to soar 92% to $29.15 billion compared to $15.15 billion in Q3 2025. Alphabet's recent introduction of Gemini 4 Argon and its new Gemini enterprise AI agent adds another potential growth catalyst as the company expands AI capabilities across Google Workspace, Search, and cloud services. However, investors will also be scrutinizing Google's AI search monetization, competition from alternative AI platforms, and rising data center expenditures, with Alphabet forecasting annual capital spending of $195-$205 billion. Microsoft's Fiscal Q1 Expectations: Azure, Copilot & AI Infrastructure Microsoft is expected to report fiscal first-quarter earnings of $4.71 per share, representing 14% growth from the prior year. Revenue is projected to rise more than 16% to $90.58 billion. Microsoft’s cloud business remains a major growth catalyst, with Microsoft Cloud revenue jumping 27% YoY to $59.3 billion last quarter, while Azure and other cloud services revenue surged 43%. Encouragingly, Microsoft expects Azure revenue growth to accelerate to 44-45% in constant currency during Q1, with Intelligent Cloud revenue projected at $40.95-$41.25 billion, representing 33-34% annual growth. Investors will also be monitoring the adoption and monetization of Microsoft 365 Copilot, its expanding AI-agent capabilities, and enterprise cloud contracts. Microsoft's growing infrastructure investments, with quarterly capital expenditures potentially exceeding $50 billion, will be another critical area to watch. While demand remains robust, higher depreciation expenses and the costs of expanding AI infrastructure could pressure cloud profit margins. Year to date, MSFT has risen 10%, while GOOGL is up a modest 3%, with both underperforming the broader indexes amid rising CapEx concerns. Over the last three years, however, Alphabet’s return of nearly 160% has outperformed the broader market, while Microsoft’s roughly 60% gain has trailed the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. At recent prices of around $320 a share for Alphabet stock and $530 for Microsoft shares, GOOGL trades at roughly 20X forward earnings, compared with 25X for MSFT. Alphabet's more attractive valuation provides some appeal, particularly considering its accelerating cloud growth and established advertising businesses. Meanwhile, Microsoft's premium reflects its enterprise software leadership, recurring revenue streams, and deeply integrated Azure and Copilot ecosystem. Both companies have compelling AI growth opportunities heading into Wednesday's earnings reports, but Alphabet appears to offer the more attractive valuation and potential upside if Google Cloud and AI monetization exceed expectations. Reflecting this, along with a more favorable trend of positive earnings estimate revisions, Alphabet stock currently sports a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), while Microsoft lands a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). title: MSFT Earnings Preview: Azure and AI Capex in Focus - tastylive
content: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) reports fiscal first quarter 2027 results on Wednesday, October 28, after the close. The stock closed Monday at $532.60 with a 52-week range of $349.20 to $553.72. That low came in late June, and shares have rallied sharply since Microsoft’s July report, when Azure growth accelerated and the stock jumped more than 13% the next day. At roughly 29.7 times trailing earnings, MSFT trades below its five-year median multiple of about 33, but the move has left little room for disappointment The implied volatility setup is moderate by earnings standards. The options market is pricing in a move of about $26, or roughly 5% of the notional value of the stock, which would put the expected range near $505 to $560 and would take MSFT through its 52-week high on the upside. History says to respect the tails. MSFT’s actual move exceeded the implied move in four of the last eight reports, including a 16% surge in April 2025 and a 13.4% jump last July. What's interesting is that the December 2026 cycle still has about 2x more implied volatility on a notional level, with a +-$46 implied range, so there is still some implied volatility priced in through the end of the year. Azure remains the engine of the story. Microsoft’s cloud platform grew 43% in fiscal Q4 and crossed $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time, and management has guided to 44% to 45% growth this quarter. Intelligent Cloud revenue is guided to $40.95 billion to $41.25 billion, up 33% to 34%. One wrinkle to watch: Microsoft re-segmented its reporting in September, so Azure growth is now measured under an updated definition. The backlog is the other headline number. Commercial RPO, the contracted revenue not yet recognized, hit $678 billion last quarter. Excluding OpenAI, it still grew 25%, which matters because concentration risk with OpenAI has been a persistent concern since early this year. Management has also said repeatedly that demand continues to exceed available capacity, so Azure growth is a function of how fast Microsoft can bring GPUs and data centers online. Capital spending is where the bull and bear debates collide. Microsoft spent $41 billion on capex in fiscal Q4, roughly two thirds on short-lived assets like GPUs and CPUs, and has guided to more than $50 billion this quarter. Calendar 2026 capex is expected to land near $175 billion. Heavy depreciation has already pressured margins: gross margin slipped to 67.6% in fiscal Q3, the lowest since 2022, and cloud gross margin was 65% last quarter. Microsoft still guided operating margin roughly flat year over year, so any slippage there will draw attention. The macro backdrop adds pressure. AI-linked stocks sold off on October 8 after a report that OpenAI’s revenue was lower than expected, and again on October 22, when MSFT fell 2.2%. Anthropic filed for its IPO on October 26, and Meta has outlined up to $95 billion in equity financing, keeping the question of how the AI buildout gets funded front and center. The bull case starts with momentum in estimates and demand. Analysts have nudged revenue estimates higher by about 1% over the past three months, with the biggest upward revisions concentrated in Intelligent Cloud, and Microsoft has a track record of beating on EPS, including a nearly 12% surprise last quarter ($4.74 versus $4.24). Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats, up from 20 million one quarter earlier, with net seat additions more than doubling. Management is also adding usage-based billing for Copilot products, which could widen monetization. Sentiment on the Street is constructive: 43 of 49 analysts rate MSFT a Buy, the consensus price target is about $592, and Oppenheimer, Scotiabank, and Truist all lifted targets this week, with two of them going to $625. Bulls also point to Microsoft’s diversified AI exposure, including its roughly 27% stake in OpenAI and a relationship with Anthropic that includes both an investment and a large Azure commitment. A beat-and-raise on Azure with stable margins would give the stock a path through $553.72 into price discovery. Bears argue that MSFT is priced for a clean beat. The stock is up about 36% in three months, and the technical picture is less convincing than the headline: MSFT has stalled three times near $546, and momentum indicators have shown bearish divergence. The January report is the cautionary tale, when shares fell as much as 12% intraday after capex jumped 66% and Microsoft disclosed that roughly 45% of its RPO was tied to OpenAI. This time, more than $50 billion in quarterly capex, falling gross margins, and nervousness about AI financing could easily outweigh a strong Azure print. Weakness outside the cloud is another drag, with More Personal Computing revenue down 4% and Xbox content and services down 5% in the last report. If Azure comes in at the low end of guidance or management signals higher spending without a matching revenue lift, a stock sitting near its highs has a long way to fall. content: Microsoft's MSFTfirst-quarter fiscal 2027 results, scheduled to be reported on Oct. 28, are likely to have been driven by accelerating growth in its cloud platform, Azure.The quarter unfolded against a backdrop of surging AI consumption, expanding agentic platforms and persistent capacity constraints that had defined the company’s cloud narrative through fiscal 2026.Click here to know how the company’s overall fiscal first-quarter fiscal 2027 performance is likely to have been. Management's guidance, issued alongside fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results, called for Azure and other cloud services revenues to grow approximately 45% in constant currency, accelerating from the fourth quarter's 43% pace. Intelligent Cloud revenues were guided between $40.95 billion and $41.25 billion, indicating 33-34% growth. Leadership indicated on the prior call that customer demand continued to exceed available supply, even as fleet efficiency gains and faster delivery of new capacity helped, with first-half fiscal 2027 growth still expected to accelerate. Microsoft added 31 data centers and another gigawatt of capacity in the fourth quarter, remaining on track to roughly double overall capacity in two years. Capital expenditure, including the lease reclassification impact from extending data center useful lives to 25 years, was expected to exceed $50 billion for the quarter, up from $41 billion in the fourth quarter. Microsoft Corporation price-eps-surprise | Microsoft Corporation Quote Heading into the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft Foundry had reached 100,000 customers, with revenues more than doubling year over year, while Microsoft 365 Copilot paid seats had surpassed 30 million. GitHub Copilot reached 50 million users, and its June shift to usage-based pricing is likely to have lifted consumption revenues during the quarter. The number of Foundry customers at a one-trillion-token annualized run rate increased fourfold year over year, while Agent 365 had nearly 40 million registered agents. These metrics suggested AI workloads were broadening beyond frontier model companies, which accounted for a little over 10% of fiscal 2026 Microsoft Cloud revenues. The quarter featured several developments that should enhance Microsoft's competitive position against other cloud giants, including Alphabet's GOOGL Google, Amazon AMZN and OracleORCL.In July, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 series became generally available in Microsoft Foundry, alongside general availability of hosted agents in Foundry Agent Service. On July 21, Microsoft expanded its partnership with Mistral, making Mistral Medium 3.5 available in Foundry and Copilot Studio across cloud, Azure Local and fully disconnected environments, and committed multibillion dollars to use part of Mistral's European GPU capacity. In August, Microsoft launched its India South Central cloud region in Hyderabad, backed by a $20.5 billion India commitment, and confirmed that its Saudi Arabia East region will become available in November. In September, Microsoft said its India data center regions are now AI-enabled and introduced Copilot Managed Runtime in preview, hosting applications built through Copilot within customers' Microsoft 365 environments. Microsoft targeted Cobalt 200 racks in over 25 data centers by July-end but has not yet confirmed reaching that target, while Maia 200 continued scaling. Collectively, these developments pointed to broadening AI adoption across models, agents and infrastructure, supporting the case for Azure growth holding near the guided level. Yet the pace of expansion also reinforced that capital intensity was not easing. Cost of revenues was guided to increase 23-24%, reflecting AI infrastructure scaling and higher component pricing, while finance lease-related interest expense was expected to push other income to roughly negative $100 million. Capacity timing and contract mix could also cause Azure growth to vary, and OpenAI-related contracts signed in the prior year were expected to create volatility in bookings and commercial remaining performance obligation growth. Why are technology stocks rising so much and is it really a good time to buy them? In July, we published an article about the 12 Best Stocks to Buy for the AI Boom in the Second Half of 2026 and AAPL ranked 11th in that article. AAPL returned 9.22% since then. So, hedge funds were right about AAPL. This article explains why hedge funds were bullish on AAPL. Before getting into our analysis, let's take a look at the business and why some investors like the stock so much. Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) remains one of the largest technology companies in the world, and the current investment debate is shifting from whether Apple can keep growing to whether its high valuation is justified as it becomes a slower-growth but more dependable technology stock. Apple reported record revenue of $109.42 billion, 16% higher than last year, with iPhone sales up 22% and earnings per share of $2.02, beating expectations. Despite these strong results, the stock fell 7.35% after earnings and kept slipping as investors focused less on what Apple just delivered and more on what it expects next: 9%-11% growth, below the 12% analysts were hoping for. With the stock trading at around 35 times earnings, that gap between a rich valuation and a slowing growth outlook is what's rattling investors. Read More: 15 AI Stocks That Are Quietly Making Investors Rich Read More: Undervalued AI Stock Poised For Massive Gains: 10000% Upside Potential The bullish case for Apple isn't built on it becoming an AI powerhouse, but on it being a safer way to stay invested in technology. While companies like Nvidia, Amazon, and Microsoft are pouring money into AI infrastructure with all the risks that come with a spending boom, Apple offers exposure to tech without betting on that cycle. Its ecosystem of iPhones, services, and wearables gives it a steady, reliable base that can keep rewarding shareholders over time, even without chasing the AI trade. The recent slowdown looks more like a supply problem than a demand problem. Apple said that memory chips, DRAM and NAND, are increasingly being funneled toward AI data centers as that industry snaps up components, which has forced Apple to limit some higher-memory device configurations. In other words, this is about chip supply being stretched thin industry-wide, not about weaker interest in Apple's products. If investors eventually look past the AI hype and back toward companies with consistent execution, Apple's steady approach could start looking more appealing. Apple's case also depends on it continuing to execute reliably even as growth slows, (see whether Apple's 35x valuation is getting ahead of its growth) and that's the piece investors will be watching closely. The real question is whether a company growing more slowly than many of its tech peers deserves to trade at such a rich multiple. Those in favor of the premium point to Apple's strong cash generation, consistent shareholder returns, and one of the most powerful consumer ecosystems in the world. But if earnings growth doesn't keep up, the market may become less willing to pay up for that stability. That said, slower growth is the biggest risk to this story. The current 9%-11% guidance may just reflect temporary supply issues, but if growth stays stuck in the single digits for longer, investors may start to worry it's a deeper problem rather than a short-term hiccup. At the same time, Apple's valuation doesn't leave much room for missteps. Adding to the uncertainty is an upcoming CEO transition, though incoming leader John Ternus brings around 25 years at Apple and a strong hardware and product background, which could help him navigate supply chain issues and future product launches. Another risk for the stock is regulatory pressure on the App Store's business model. Apple's ecosystem supports repeat spending, but regulators and courts are challenging how it controls app distribution and collects commissions. Apple has already changed its European platform rules to allow alternative distribution and payment options. If more transactions move outside its payment system, Apple could collect less revenue from the same customer activity. Defending its fee structure also brings legal costs and uncertainty. These pressures could weaken earnings even if device demand remains healthy. In our opinion, Apple's premium valuation becomes harder to justify if the ecosystem remains popular but generates less profit from each user. That near-flat change suggests institutional investors are neither piling in nor backing away, reflecting steady confidence rather than any dramatic shift in sentiment. title: Microsoft Is Paying Workers to Leave So It Can Pay for AI - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Microsoft just offered buyouts to roughly a quarter of its entire workforce, and the announcement never once mentions AI or cost cutting. The real reason hiding in the spending figures tells a very different story. On Monday, October 26, 2026, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees. That is roughly 27% of the 223,000 people it employed full-time as of June 30. The stock rose 1.54% to $532.60 and was little changed after hours at $532.45, leaving the company worth about $3.95 trillion. The offer comes as AI spending rises fast. Microsoft spent $115.95 billion on capital expenditures in fiscal 2026, up 79.62%, while free cash flow fell 6.46%. Microsoft’s announcement never mentions AI or cost cutting. The link to AI comes from the spending figures and the teams invited to leave, and that evidence is strong enough to take seriously. The company’s post, “Introducing a Voluntary Exit Offer,” was signed by Amy Coleman as executive vice president and chief people officer. It describes a time-limited offer for employees at level 70 and below on participating teams in the U.S., Canada, India, and the U.K. Participation “varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs,” and the company added, “The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us… We’ll learn from it.” Uptake, total cost and exact severance terms were not disclosed, but terms are reportedly similar to standard severance, and eligible staff reportedly have until early December to accept, with departures on December 31. Participating parts reportedly include Xbox, Windows, Copilot and Finance. Data center, sales, and marketing staff are largely left out, which means the teams that build and sell AI capacity are protected. This is also the third workforce move of the year. An April retirement program covered 8,750 U.S. workers and drew acceptance above 30%, and in July Microsoft cut 4,800 jobs, or 2.1% of staff, mostly in Xbox. Going from a targeted retirement offer to layoffs to a broad exit offer looks like a structural reset. A one-time trim would not follow that sequence. Industry data center investment is likely to top $700 billion this year. In July, CFO Amy Hood put Microsoft’s calendar-2026 capex at about $175 billion. The earlier figure was $190 billion, and it came down only because longer asset lives moved some leases out of capex. Capex hit about $41 billion in the June quarter, and the forecast for the September quarter was more than $50 billion. Depreciation, the annual expense charged as that equipment wears out, weighs on margins for years. Payroll is the largest cost management can change quickly. Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC) rates the stock Overweight with a $725 target. It estimated that if one-third of eligible workers accept, operating margin would gain about 2 percentage points a year. The one-third figure is an assumption, though April’s uptake makes it plausible. Fiscal first-quarter results are expected after the close on Wednesday, October 28. Analysts expect EPS of $4.7199 on revenue of about $90.75 billion. The key questions are clear. Investors want to know whether management can quantify the offer’s charges or savings, whether capex guidance rises again, and whether cloud growth can stay ahead of depreciation. Azure grew 43% last quarter, commercial backlog reached $678 billion, and demand still tops capacity. A lower payroll in slower units makes that expansion cheaper to carry. The main risks are clear. The best people may be the ones who leave, morale in Xbox and Windows could suffer, and the savings are small next to quarterly capex. The stock trades below its $553.72 52-week high. The margin case was wrong. That would be the outcome if the October 28 report increases capex without quantifying the offer’s savings, and shares have not recaptured that high by December 31. Microsoft has become the latest large company to reduce its workforce over the artificial intelligence boom, offering buyouts to tens of thousands of employees. The company said on Monday that some 60,000 employees are eligible for the buyout. Those reached are in the U.S., Canada, India and the UK and have an experience level of 70 or below. Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, said in a memo that the program "reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter." "This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program," she added. Those who will accept the offer must make the decision over the next weeks and will leave at the end of the year. The company's stock is climbing on Monday, gaining almost 1.5% at 2:33 p.m. ET amid a session of broad gains. American Express and Barclays announced thousands of layoffs last week, citing AI as a main reason. The former's CEO, Stephen Squeri, said on Friday that the company will eliminate 5% of the global workforce, which at the end of last year amounted to some 77,000 employees. "We've got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we needed to become more agile and efficient organization," Squeri said when presenting the company's quarterly results. "We believe this exercise will help us operate and execute more effectively and give us greater capacity to invest in our business priorities," he added. The announcement came a day after Barclays announced plans to eliminate some 5,000 jobs as it turns to AI and organizational changes to lower costs and free up money for investment. The reductions, disclosed Thursday alongside its third-quarter results, will fall heavily on support operations. About 60% of the cuts are expected to affect support functions, including developers, according to the bank's earnings presentation. The announcement puts technology workers among those exposed to the restructuring, alongside other employees supporting the bank's operations. Barclays described the changes as part of a broader effort to simplify its organization and improve efficiency through technology. The bank expects the workforce reductions to be completed by the end of the year. Chief Financial Officer Anna Cross told reporters that approximately 1,000 positions had already been eliminated, with another 4,000 expected to go before year-end. The broader picture shows a contrasting image. New applications for U.S. unemployment benefits have fallen to one of their lowest levels in more than five decades, but a closer look at the labor market reveals a difficult reality for Americans who are searching for work. Initial claims dropped by 6,000 to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 in the week ending Oct. 17, according to figures released Thursday by the U.S. Department of Labor. That was the lowest reading since July, when claims reached 189,000, a level not seen since 1969. But at the same time, about 1.94 million Americans had been unemployed for 27 weeks or longer in September, representing 27.1% of all unemployed workers, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' September employment report. The number was little changed from August, but it means more than one in four unemployed Americans had been without work for at least six months. title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push - CNBC
content:
Microsoft said Monday that it’s offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency. The software maker announced a new voluntary exit offer for certain workers in the U.S., Canada, India and the United Kingdom at its experience level of 70 or below. Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter. The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft’s total workforce of 223,000 people. Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies. Capital expenditures for the September quarter should exceed $50 billion, Microsoft said in July. In the same quarter a year ago, capital spending and finance leases came to $34.9 billion. That’s put a strain on Microsoft’s finances. In April, it announced a first-ever voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for. Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees. “The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees. “This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program.” Microsoft is in the midst of a business model transformation, increasingly trying to charge clients based on how much AI they actually use. It has armed programmers, sellers and supply chain workers with AI tools and observed noticeable results. At the same time, the 51-year-old maker of Windows and Office wants to ensure that it has the right talent to go after its most compelling new growth opportunities. The idea is to make the shift without weakening Microsoft’s financial profile. In the second quarter, cloud rivals Alphabet and Amazon both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed $19.64 billion in positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year. Some marketing, sales and engineering teams have decided not to participate in the new buyout, the person said. Employees must decide whether to take the offer in early December, and those participating will leave on Dec. 31, the person added. More than 30% of those who could join the voluntary retirement program went ahead with it, Microsoft said in July. But that was open to those at the senior director level of 67 and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan. The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around. On Wednesday, Microsoft is scheduled to report third-quarter results. title: Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy Microsoft Stock - The Motley Fool
content: Earnings jumped 22% last fiscal year. Why would I still want the stock around 12% cheaper? Microsoft (MSFT -0.24%) closed at a record $543.45 on Oct. 13, and it hasn't moved far since. Shares trade near $530 as of this writing, about 2% off the high. Microsoft posts results for the fiscal first quarter of 2027 (the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026) after the market closes on Wednesday, Oct. 28. The company has earned a good chunk of that climb. Microsoft's adjusted earnings per share jumped 22% for fiscal 2026, which ended June 30. But at today's price, shares cost about 31 times those earnings. It's a steep price for a business whose own guidance suggests slower growth right as its capital spending keeps rising. I'd buy the stock at about $465 a share, roughly 12% under where it trades now. Microsoft's fiscal 2026 was impressive by nearly any measure. Revenue grew 18% to $331.8 billion, and operating income climbed 21% to $155.2 billion. Non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share, which strip out the effect of Microsoft's investments in OpenAI, increased 22% to $17.28. And the pace held up all year, with adjusted earnings per share up 23% year over year in both the first and fourth quarters of fiscal 2026. But the stock price already reflects much of that. With shares around $530, Microsoft trades at about 31 times its fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings. On reported earnings of $17.95 per share, it's about 30. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,807,778 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. The price-to-earnings ratio for the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.60%) on its reported earnings is about 26. The premium is easier to defend when earnings rise 22% a year. And management's forecast for the September quarter suggests growth is slowing, at least a little. Microsoft sees revenue between $89.85 billion and $90.95 billion, cost of revenue between $29.6 billion and $29.8 billion, and operating expenses between $16.8 billion and $16.9 billion. At these levels, operating income would climb around 14% to 17% from the year-ago quarter's $38.0 billion. This compares to year-over-year growth of 24%, 21%, 20%, and 18% over the four quarters of fiscal 2026. In short, operating income growth has slowed every quarter for a year, and the guidance shows it slowing again. The spending is the bigger reason I want a discount. Cash from operations grew a strong 34% in fiscal 2026, to about $183 billion. But Microsoft also spent almost $116 billion on additions to property and equipment, so free cash flow dipped about 6% to roughly $67 billion. What's more, management expects capital expenditures of about $175 billion in calendar 2026. "[W]e expect to remain free cash flow positive in FY27," chief financial officer Amy Hood said on Microsoft's earnings call in July. It's arguably a low bar -- Microsoft produced around $67 billion in free cash flow last fiscal year. My buy price starts with the $17.28 Microsoft earned per share last fiscal year on an adjusted basis. I'd pay a price-to-earnings multiple of around 27 on that number, which comes out to about $465 a share. At that price, Microsoft's price-to-earnings ratio on reported earnings would be about 26, on par with the S&P 500's. I think paying around the market's valuation multiple is fair for a business whose earnings growth looks set to cool toward the mid-teens as its spending keeps climbing. Shares last closed under $465 on July 31, two days after the company's fiscal fourth-quarter report pushed the stock sharply higher. The Oct. 28 report might shift my price in two ways. The first is earnings. Because my price is linked to trailing adjusted earnings per share, every strong quarter lifts it. Management's guidance suggests operating income growth of a bit over 15% at the midpoint. If adjusted earnings per share gained 15% from the year-ago period's $4.13, trailing adjusted earnings per share would reach around $17.90, and my buy price would rise to about $483. The second is Azure, Microsoft's cloud computing platform. As I wrote earlier this month, I think the stock needs Azure's growth to stay above 40%. If Azure falls short, or if free cash flow keeps dropping, I'd want to pay a lower price-to-earnings ratio than 27, and my buy price would fall with it. Would I buy Microsoft stock before Oct. 28? Not at roughly $530. Sure, a strong report might raise my buy price, and shares may never drop as low as $465. But at about 31 times adjusted earnings, I think the stock already reflects most of the good news. I'd consider buying closer to $465.
